title: Stack and Heap

answers: The move must copy exactly three machine words as observable work.
Ownership transfers without cloning every element or allocating a second buffer.
Each element is copied into a newly allocated destination buffer.
writing.exampleCaption: The owned allocation is retained across this move; this does not measure emitted machine instructions.
writing.explanation:
Storage location and ownership are separate. A Vec handle can be a local, a field inside another allocation or optimized away. For a nonempty u8 vector with allocated capacity, moving the Vec transfers its existing buffer; no fixed count of machine instructions or copied bytes follows.

A function call commonly creates a stack frame containing local values or handles whose sizes are known to the compiler. Heap allocation supports values whose storage needs to live independently of a particular stack frame or whose size is chosen at runtime. But ownership and physical location are separate questions. A `Vec<T>` value holds a pointer, length, and capacity as a small handle; its elements usually live in a heap allocation. Moving the `Vec` handle transfers ownership of that allocation without copying every element.

Cloning a `Vec` is different: it creates another allocation and copies or clones elements. A `Box<T>` puts a T allocation on the heap but has one owner. A `String` is a growable UTF-8 buffer with a small handle. A fixed array can live inside a stack frame, inside a heap allocation, or inside another struct depending on where its owner is stored. Do not claim that every dynamically sized value automatically goes to the heap or that stack memory is always faster for every use.

In an interview, draw the owner’s handle and the allocation, then trace a move, a borrow, and a clone. Explain when Drop releases the allocation. Mention recursion and stack-size limits if relevant, but keep the answer tied to the code at hand. If asked about performance, say that allocation patterns, cache locality, and copying cost matter more than a slogan about stack versus heap. Measure a realistic workload before changing representation.

A borrow does not move the allocation at all; it creates temporary access to the existing value. Use this contrast with move and clone in the diagram. Also mention that stack overflow is possible with deep recursion or large local arrays, even though stack allocation itself is cheap in the common case.

Interview follow-up: How do Vec::clone, a borrowed slice and a moved Vec differ? What changes if the Vec handle is itself a field in a heap allocation?
writing.feedback: Vec has pointer, length and capacity metadata, but its field layout/order and emitted move instructions are not fixed here. The handle need not be physically on a stack; optimization may eliminate a move.
writing.question: What does moving this Vec guarantee about its elements and allocation?
writing.rule: A move transfers ownership; handle placement and optimized instructions are not language guarantees.
writing.success: You can explain why moving a `String` is cheap but cloning it is not.
